utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Name, please?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Ehsan Bajwa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nationality?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: From Pakistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Education?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: BA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I did my BA degree at the University of Punjab in Lahore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you join the police force?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were how old?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: At that time, I was 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're now?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Thirty-two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you join as an officer?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, as a commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you promoted within five or six years to the rank of superintendent?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, I was, in 1995 to be exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that as young an age as an officer in Pakistan can reach the rank of superintendent?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you join the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: In August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same year you became a superintendent?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's true. Almost eight months after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since then ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the speakers to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: ... renewals of your initial contract have you just had?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I just received the fifth one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of working for the Tribunal, have you collected or have you taken many witness statements?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. I failed to put my headphones on. I will do so. Was one of the statements you took the statement from Muhamed Mujezinovic, the statement being taken on the 3rd of February, 1997?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that occasion were you working together with Gregory Kehoe, one of the lawyers of the institution, and were you assisted by Lejla Avdagic, an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did work with Greg Kehoe and was assisted by Lejla Avdagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please tell us the process whereby the witness statement was taken.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: The way a witness statement is taken differs from situation to situation. It was a situation where the witness had already been interviewed on previous occasions, so it was a supplementary statement. The purpose of the interview, for one, was that Mr. Greg Kehoe would be able to gain some personal impression of the witness. Secondly, we wanted to clarify some of the points and issues that did arise from his previous statements. So we introduced ourselves, because I personally, and I believe that's true for Mr. Greg Kehoe as well, we had not met him before, so we introduced ourselves as a lawyer and investigator from ICTY, and we explained what the purpose of this interview was, why were we meeting yet another time and talking about those things. Lejla Avdagic was, of course, interpreting for us, and the interview lasted for about six, seven hours. I had the statement that the witness had given previously in July 1995, I believe, taken by Simon Leach. I had that statement before me. I would raise a matter from that statement with the witness, and he would recount the story that he told to the previous investigator. I would see to what extent his renarration, his recounting, was in keeping with what he said before, and I would seek explanations if there was some minor differences. If there were matters that had not been addressed and in my view should have been addressed, I would ask him questions regarding that. I did indeed prepare a statement on the basis of that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the statement prepared there and then, and if so, how, by hand, on a laptop or what?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed the statement was prepared contemporaneously with the interview and it was on a laptop computer that the statement was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the conclusion of the preparation of the statement, was Dr. Mujenznovic given an opportunity to consider the statement and, if so, how was he given that opportunity?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, he was given that opportunity. It was Lejla Avdajic, our interpreter, who read that statement back to the witness, and we asked him, is it in keeping with what he had said. Is it a true representation of what he had said, and he agreed that yes, it was. Then we asked him to sign it, and he did indeed sign the signature, as did I, and my interpreter Lejla Avdajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember anything being said on that occasion about translations, either the translation on that occasion or any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: As I read this statement that I recorded, there was one point where the witness did say something about the translation on the previous occasion. I do not have an exact recollection of what exactly he did say, but he said something to the effect that the translation was not as good on the previous occasion. The point at which I can recall that while reading in the statement is where that witness mentions the number of people being held in detention and as it was given to him during the meeting with Mario Cerkez. In his interview with me, the witness said that the number of people who were being held in detention, as alleged by Mario Cerkez, was 2.223. I said, "But in your brief statement to Simon Leach during July 1995, you just said more than 2.000 and now you are saying 2.223. How would you account for this precision?" I believe that it was at that point that he said something -- he made some remark about the quality of translation on that previous occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. As to the man Darko Kraljevic, do you have any present vivid recollection of his speaking of Darko Kraljevic at all?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall that one of the things that I had wanted to address during this meeting was Darko Kraljevic. He had indeed spoke about Darko Kraljevic, his activities, and Dr. Mujenznovic's rapport with Darko Kraljevic because of his having treated Darko Kraljevic. In his previous statement with Simon Leach he had spoken about that. There were sides and there were areas of that exchange that I wanted to clarify, so I did indeed speak with him about Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It happens that you're also the investigator who took some of the statements that relate to the town or village of Tulica.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As of today, have you reconsidered those statements in any detail or not?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: No. I haven't had a chance to review those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, if there is any question I ask you that you don't understand, would you please let me know; all right? We'll both have to slow down for the translators.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I will try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So will I. Now, first, sir, your responsibility as a member of the OTP investigation unit is to conduct investigations and develop prosecution briefs; correct?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Conduct investigations, yes; insofar as developing prosecution briefs is concerned, the members of the team from the prosecution section who are qualified lawyers, they have a greater role in that process than investigative members of that team do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So you have no role in developing the prosecution brief?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Sometimes we are asked to summarise witness statements and things that are directly in relation to the work that we did, and we do, indeed, do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The investigative team assesses all the relevant material for those briefs, ensuring that all relevant evidence has been assembled and included in the brief in order to establish such element of each charge, as well as prepare the actual brief for the prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, in constant consultation with the legal members of the team, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sure. Your focus is to aid and assist the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You're aware, of course, that Dr. Mujezinovic had multiple statements taken?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the fact that he had been interviewed in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Just as with all the other persons you interview, the purpose of taking a statement is to get the facts?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You're not interested in rumours?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course not, except that in one's evaluation of evidence, there is hearsay which might as well be characterised as rumour, and there are some things that a witness has experienced directly. So hearsay has evidential importance, so, of course, we do not just discount material that might otherwise be characterised as rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. The result is, when you're gathering facts, you let the person talk to you and tell you what he or she has to say?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That may include hearsay?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Double hearsay?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: General rumour?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And at some point, you may ferret out that which is hearsay and rumour, if you have a chance?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes. Not only is it a question of chance, but under the existing protocols and practice directions within the investigation section, we are required to make it very clear in the body of the statement what it is that the witness is saying on the basis of personal, direct knowledge and what is it that's based on his exchanges with somebody else, which is hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. We can agree, however, as a practical matter in Bosnia, sometimes that becomes difficult?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Well, it's a question of how scrupulously an investigator, whoever is interviewing, pursues that question, and the question of relative importance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, Mr. Stein. I should like to hear from the witness. You asked him, when taking down the statement, does he take note whether it is hearsay, double hearsay, or rumour. When he records hearsay, double hearsay, and rumours, does he mention in the statement that he takes down that it is hearsay, double hearsay, or rumour in those cases, that the person heard something from another person or that a person said that it was on the basis of a rumour that he learnt it? So does he take down the source of the information obtained from his interlocutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, I believe the Judge's question is clear.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course, whenever there is hearsay, we are required to explicitly record in the body of the statement "I heard this being said." Sometimes it is possible for the witness who is talking to us to identify the person concerned who said that. For instance, in the statement under consideration here, Darko Kraljevic says something to Dr. Mujezinovic, and here we are in a position to identify the source of this hearsay, so we have identified that. Sometimes it is something just being said, and the witness has an impression that this was being bandied about, this was something that was being talked over, and that it was explicitly mentioned that way in the body of the statement, that I heard this being said, and then the witness expresses his or her inability to specifically point out the person who is the source of that rumour or that hearsay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) So if I have understood you correctly, you faithfully reproduce what the witness tells you, including the source of the information that he is conveying?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Following up on that, that's the goal that you personally aspire to; correct?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course, and many times, we are, indeed, able to get very near to the achievement of that goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sure. And many times not?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: There might be odd instances where some statement does leave a certain degree of ambiguity which one trusts can be sorted out in the course of direct testimony in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And there are 150 or 200 persons just like you working for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I'm not certain as to the exact number of investigators, and I believe that's what you mean by "you persons."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the total number of us are. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It's certainly more than half a dozen?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course, it is, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I will never be "Your Honour," believe me. Are all the individuals who are doing investigative work similarly trained as to you, police officers who became investigators, or do they have a variety of different backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course they have a variety of different backgrounds and a variety of various police systems and variety of experiences, and that actually is very helpful to the quality of product that this action finally comes up with, because a variety of different experiences are brought to bear on the quality of work that's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. We can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first thing is you rebuked the witness. I think he was being polite towards the Court, not being polite to you, but that's as may be. Could you slow down a bit, Mr. Bajwa, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try my best, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's difficult for the interpreters otherwise. Mr. Stein, where are we going on this? Let me just say this: You know what the rules are, and the witness came simply to talk about one statement. Now, obviously some leeway would be allowed. If you want to explore generally the taking of statements, we'll let you do that, provided it doesn't take up too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I thought it might be relevant given what's before us, and I don't want to take up a lot of time with it at all, maybe one or two more questions I would like to get into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this: The conditions of taking the interviews that you and your colleagues take, I imagine, are somewhat difficult when you're in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Difficult in the sense that at times one would like to explore matters at greater length, and then given the resource constraints and the time constraints, probably some of the statements do not explore matters to the same length that one would have wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Are there instances in which individuals appear with their families or other people and want to interview in that process, with more than one person present?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: It's a requirement under the protocol in the practice direction within the investigation section that every effort will be made that other than a witness, there is nobody else present, of course, the investigator and the interpreter, unless it is absolutely necessary to furnish some kind of moral support to the witness and the witness insists on that, but it is an explicit direction that the investigator will try to discourage that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you find that despite your directions that that often happens?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I have spent four years with the Tribunal, and there are scores and scores of statements that I have recorded, and not on one occasion have I had a problem of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Do you find, and this is my last general question, that there is a difficulty among your interviewees separating their personal knowledge from the general knowledge or community belief?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I think it will be very difficult to generalise in this area. There are witnesses who have a certain degree of difficulty, but there are other witnesses who do not have that, and I think that statements and the oral testimony in the court more or less does reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. With regard to the statement you made on this issue, do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That statement was made when, sir?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: If you're referring to my statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: -- it was made about two weeks ago, and I apologise, but probably the body of the statement does not mention the date on which it was made, but it was about two weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That was made for the purpose of this particular hearing?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, you took Dr. Mujezinovic's statement and you took about six hours to take it?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. He had previously to that given a statement on March 1, 1995 to Mr. Leach and Mr. Gerns. You were aware of that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I was aware of the statement, and I had that statement in front of me during this interview that took place in February, and I understand that that statement was taken in July, not March. Actually, I do have a copy of that statement here, and it says "13 July" and "16 July, 1995." So this is the statement that I had before me when I recorded this supplementary statement myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's be clear. The Office of the Prosecutor has furnished us with two statements. One is an information provided on 1 March, 1995, unsigned, looks like a rough draft. Have you ever seen that?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: May I know who that statement is recorded by, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Simon Leach and John Gerns?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's not the one. I was aware of the existence of that statement, but I knew that after the taking of that statement, another more complete and more comprehensive statement had been taken, so I based my interview on the statement that was taken subsequent to that one, and that was in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. We'll go there in a second. But as of the March 1, 1995 interview with Leach and Gerns, I've been saying "Kearns," it's "Gerns," "G-E-R-N-S," you are not aware as to whether or not, when this statement was transcribed to English, Dr. Mujezinovic complained about the translation?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Similarly, as to when the July 13/16 statement was taken, and that is a statement taken again by Simon Leach and an interpreter named Mubina van Veen-Isovic?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When that statement was finished, you're not aware whether Dr. Mujezinovic said, "I'm unhappy with the translations" or not?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Except for the fact that when I spoke with Dr. Mujezinovic and when he mentioned the number of detainees and when I put my question to him, he did say something to the effect that on the previous occasion, the translation was not probably as fluent as on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fine. Did you also hear from Dr. Mujezinovic on that occasion that the translators had promised to change his statement?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. He has said to the Court that he had told the translators all along of complications with these translations, and they said they would change the statements.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: It's not that I don't recall that. It is that he did not say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: To you. As to whether or not he said it in July to Mr. Leach and the interpreter you're unaware?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I'm absolutely unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This addendum for you and Mr. Kehoe was for his testimony in Blaskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the purposes in view, but of course, he being a witness who spoke of matters that were of common relevance to many cases, so it did have greater relevance than that but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. This statement consists of four pages? That's the statement dated 3 February, '97.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So after a six-hour interview we end up with four pages.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There certainly isn't a verbatim transcript of everything that was said in that six hours?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It is your selective interpretation of that which was important to your second interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I wouldn't say "selective interpretation." What happened is that he had given a statement before, and we wanted to see him saying the same things, going over the same things without this statement being read over to him again. So we would prompt him on an issue, and then he would recount the story as he had done to Mr. Simon Leach. Then we would hear to what extent what he is saying is faithfully recorded in his previous statement. Only where some issue remained unaddressed would it eventually be incorporated into the statement that I took, four-page statement. So a substantial portion that have time of six hours was spent just making sure the previous statement is sufficiently confirmed by him, and so that we can see what are the points that we need to thrash further with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In other words, you were making him a better witness in preparation for trial.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know that's a fair comment at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this: Did you carry with you a tape recorder?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Does anybody from the OTP tape record the statements as they're given?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Except when the person being interviewed is a suspect, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. When Dr. Mujenznovic came to testify in this case, did you have occasion to see him at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to participate in his proofing at all?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If Dr. Mujenznovic has testified in front of this Tribunal that he consistently complained about the translations, I gather it's your view that those complaints weren't aired to you?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Of course not. Not at all. It was just a cursory reference that he made and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And if he says that relative to Mr. Kraljevic and other issues he made substantial substantive complaints, you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: As an interview that I conducted with him is concerned, I did not feel that there was any necessity for me to go over everything again in my statement, so no, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And as to the others, you're unaware?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As soon as I find something, I have one other question. I'd like to turn to the statement that you have in front of you, which is the statement of two weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were asked to prepare this statement for this proceeding?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: What I was exactly told was that there was a certain issue arising from Mujezinovic's testimony and nothing more than that. I asked, "May I refer to the transcript of what happened in the court?" I was explicitly told not to do that. So I was absolutely in the dark what the whole issue was about. I was just told, "You should prepare a statement concerning the circumstances in which you took this statement." So it was some kind of a -- sort of a groping statement that I made. I was not very sure. "What am I supposed to write about?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. And yet the statement contains six paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There's nothing in the six paragraphs indicating that Dr. Mujenznovic complained about the statement with respect to Mr. Kraljevic or anything else?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I think that I would have created an impression that that was not really something that was discussed between us and Mujezinovic as something of an issue. So it didn't really strike me that there is something that would have become an issue here. So that's why the statement does not address that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is I'm correct, there's nothing in your statement addressing Dr. Mujenznovic complaining about the translations?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Further, in the interview you conducted, there's no recordation anywhere that Mujenznovic complained about the translation at any time?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: The exact point he spoke to us about translation was not more than 2.000 people but 2.223 people, and I faithfully recorded that number in my statement, but not his observation that this translation on the previous occasion was not as fluent and as effortless as it was on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That latter part was left out?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bajwa, would you tell us again when it was that you interviewed Dr. Mujenznovic, please?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: It was on the 3rd of February, 1997, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination? I'm sorry. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sir, I represent Mario Cerkez. My name is Bozidar Kovacic and I am an attorney from Rijeka. On the occasion that we have just discussed and what you mention in your statement, when you met Dr. Mujenznovic, during that interview which lasted about six hours, as you have told us, did you ever indicate that the interview was for a particular case or, rather, which case the interview was for?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I cannot recall that I referred to particular cases on that occasion. No, I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have explained to us, a moment ago, but let me asking, as a rule, does the witness that you're interviewing know for what case he is testifying or, rather, in which case you intend to use his testimony for?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Under the standing procedures within the investigation section, whenever we see a witness for the first time we are supposed to explain the mandate of the Tribunal to that witness and then explain that we are representing the Tribunal and we would be interested in some of the experiences that witness has been through or witness has observed, but we are not required to specify the case. That's number one. Number two, it's difficult to specify cases because it depends on at what point in time you are meeting that witness. At times you are meeting that witness and you yourself do not know that there's a case or you are going to have a case at all. So before the indictment -- and then indictment takes place. So subsequently you may have an idea of what your conversation is going to be about. So it depends. As answer, under existing standing procedures, it is not requisite that we explain what the case is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, as a result, the witness does not know against which accused he is testifying?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: What we are required to explain and what one can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you --

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well from your explanation, the witness, as a rule, does not know against which of the accused he will be called to testify.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: He would know that he would be called to testify but not necessarily which accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke to Dr. Mujenznovic on the 3rd of February, 1997, the indictment against Blaskic and others was already issued.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you, on that occasion, tell the witness that an indictment exists? You said that together with Mr. Kehoe you had come for him to get an impression about that witness. Did you tell him then which case he was going to be called for?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Just as I said before, I have no recollection of raising that matter with him, but there's just one more qualification I'd like to add to that, which is this witness had been spoken to before that occasion on a couple of times, so it was -- I think it could have been that it was a tacit understanding that we are talking about in the context of the Lasva Valley indictments, but I do not have a clear recollection of that, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From what you have told us so far, I take it that you consider yourself to be a conscientious investigator.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's an ideal that I would like to strive after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the place and date a statement is given on are important or not?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: They are important. Things have to be defined in terms of time and space.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, it was noted that you didn't put the date or the place even on your own statement.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes. That's a lapse on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Lapses are understandable. Perhaps you were unexpectedly called by my learned friend, the Prosecutor, and you did it in great haste, and that is the explanation why you forgot to note the date and the place?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: No. I think it was more out of a feeling of complete ignorance that what is it about than anything else, any impression of haste about it, that this lapse might have resulted from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the examination by Mr. Stein and from your statement, we have been able to understand the actual technology of taking interviews, but there is one point that is not clear to me. So may I summarise and then you confirm for me? Using a specific example, the witness speaks Croatian, or Bosnian, or Serbian. It doesn't matter. Then the interpreter interprets orally what he says and then you take that down on your laptop; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: There's just one minor factor here, that is while the witness is speaking, the interpreter takes down certain notes. And an effort is made that the witness is not permitted to speak for very long, and he is interrupted so it could be of a manageable size, the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in any event, the witness speaks in Bosnian, Croatian, or Serbian, then in summary form the interpreter interprets it into English, and you take that down on your laptop.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: It is one point. In the existing practice direction in the investigation section, the investigator is required to tell the interpreter that he is to interpret verbatim, not paraphrasing. There is no element of paraphrasing. That's number one. Number two, the witness is not permitted to speak too long, so it's a manageable size. With those qualifications, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then the other way round. You said that the witness was informed of what has been taken down. So now you will be speaking English, the interpreter will be interpreting into Croatian for the benefit of the witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the witness has the ability to check the accuracy of his statement, accuracy of the way it was noted down only on the basis of the oral interpretation given.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I apologise. The point escapes me. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase. The witness, at the end, signs his statement. It is written in English. It is written in the English language because you wrote it down on your laptop. The interpreter reads it out to the witness in Croatian, and then after that the witness agrees that that is his statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To make quite sure, does the witness ever see his statement in Croatian in writing as a document?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I believe that at some point before testifying, the translation section probably translates the statements back into Serbo-Croatian. I'm not certain about that, but this is my impression. Apart from that, immediately after the conclusion of the interview and the recording of the statement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, sir, in organisational terms, who is your superior? You do not have to give me the name, of course, but the title. Who has the superior position above yours in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: It would be a team leader, by designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And his superior?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: It would be an investigations commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And his superior? And his superior?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Chief of investigations would be in charge of the investigations section which is a component within the Office of the Prosecutor, at the apex of that office is the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I understand. So in hierarchical terms, the investigators are a section within the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are not an independent institution?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Depends on how do we look at the word "Independence".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Kovacic, where are we going? What is the point of these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I should like to see whether we can consider the investigator being a completely independent body over which the Prosecutor and no one else has any influence, that is, independent in collecting information and providing it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bajwa, did anyone influence you -- if this seems to be the point -- did anybody influence you in taking this statement?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have described in some detail the procedure, and I understand it and I have been able to see it from your statements, but tell us, please, in addition to the statement of the witness that has been noted down, or the substance of that statement, do you hand over for further processing any personal notes or comments like the witness appears to be convincing, he's not convincing, he's eloquent in speech, he's sure of himself, he's unsure of himself, things that cannot be seen just by merely reading through the statement?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: As a question of personal custom, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that means my learned friends, the Prosecutors, who continue working on the basis of this paper that you gave them, they don't know whether he is convincing, eloquent, an educated man, or a man who is unsure of himself, who stammers, et cetera, they have no information of that kind?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I mention in my statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Kovacic, I think we are going astray in this cross-examination, because we have started from the problem of a witness, because it was raised in the filings, that witness being Mr. Mujezinovic, and now we're covering the whole issue of investigations, the Prosecution, and how these things function, but that is not the place to do so. If we're talking about the functioning of the Prosecutor or the investigator, it needs to be said in advance. So I'm asking you, as I have already done before, to limit yourself to this statement. Otherwise, we're going to go beyond the scope of the subject we're dealing with today, and you know we have many other things to address later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Of course, Your Honour. I will abide by that, but I see no reason why this witness was brought here. But as he has been brought here, I'm interested in learning how these things are done, but I will leave out a number of questions that I had planned to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of the discrepancies that arose here and prompted all this, would you please tell us, you speak to the witness in the way we have described, you take down what he has said. If the witness says something that is completely unexpected, that is completely contradictory to what you have already heard on the same subject from other witnesses, do you then take any steps, on your own initiative, to tell that witness that the fact that he has given simply doesn't seem to stand, or do you take steps to verify the veracity of that statement? What are your competencies in that regard?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: There will be two ways to deal with that situation. One way would be to see the internal consistency of what the witness is saying. To what extent there is a coherence, internal coherence, in what he's saying, and that would be talking about what he has said. Then if there are other sources of information and it's quite clear to the investigator that on the basis of other information that the investigator has there might be an element of ignorance in what the witness is saying, at times you confront the witness with that but, "On the basis of this, this, this, I know this. How do you deal with that?" Then you see how a witness responds to that. On certain other occasions you just faithfully record what the witness has said and then see how can that be afterwards developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From witness Mujezinovic, in February '97, you heard a figure, when quoting Cerkez, 2.223 people detained in the cinema hall. At that time, the Blaskic indictment had already been issued and you had already spoken to other witnesses, and not one of them mentioned a figure anywhere near that one. Did you confront Dr. Mujenznovic with this fact?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Well, I was not aware at that time that anybody else had given a specific figure on this. So people had generally said many people. Some people have said hundreds of people. So I was not quite astonished about the figure that Mujezinovic was given. Given the population figures of Vitez, it was not a sort of inconceivable figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that the purpose of the interview, the basic purpose, was to clarify, and explain, and broaden the earlier statement given by Mujezinovic earlier on, and it is on the basis of that statement that you posed your questions.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If you looked at his 1995 statement and asked questions on that basis, then you must have noticed another discrepancy. Do you recollect that you may have asked him for an explanation regarding who, among those three present of the first talk mentioned when he said Pero Skopljak, Ivo Santic, and Mario Cerkez were present, who exactly had mentioned the number of 2.300, roughly, because this cannot be seen from the 1995 statement.

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Well, in the statement that I recorded, it's clearly said that Mario Cerkez said that, so I did not pursue that point beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you compared it with the statement of 1995. You said that, in fact, you interviewed him on the basis of that statement, asking him questions about things that were not clear or logical, so that the 1997 statement is a complement to the 1995 statement, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Would you please direct me, sir, to the concerned portion of the 1995 statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: 1995, it would be the part of the statement --

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: In 1995, page number 6, the statement recorded in July 1995, page number 6, the 22nd line from the top, and it says: "Cerkez told me that they had more than 2.200 arrested persons." So since I did not see any discrepancy here, he was pretty specific on the identity of the person who was mentioning the numbers to him, so I didn't see any discrepancy for me to ask him about, presumably because I do not exactly recall all the details of that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose you're right. It was another statement from 1995 and not this one. I do apologise. To go back very briefly to another matter that we've already touched upon, in this particular case, regarding the witness Dr. Mujezinovic, was there anywhere a comment on your part as a recommendation to the Prosecution regarding the quality of that witness?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few matters arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the reading back of statements of witnesses is concerned, how seriously or otherwise is that exercise undertaken?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: It's serious enough for a specific interpreter's certificate being incorporated in the standard format of a statement, and the fact that reading back is specifically mentioned in the witness's acknowledgement at the end of each standard format of a statement, to have been incorporated, so it's taken very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about your instructions when you prepared the statement that's been served in respect of today's hearings. You've told us how you weren't to consult the transcript and so on. Have you since then, before coming to give evidence, been asked whether you had any recollection of any issue of translation?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes, I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you then gave evidence today about what you recalled about translation?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you also asked whether you had any recollection of Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked one rather oblique question about Kraljevic; nevertheless, can you just tell, please, the Chamber what your recollection of references to Kraljevic in this statement were?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: The previous statement recorded by Mr. Leach had incorporated a story about Kraljevic mentioning people insisting on him putting Muslim houses on fire and creating anarchy in Vitez, something to that effect, and one of the things that I wanted to do during this interview was to put that event in some context. So I asked Mujezinovic, "How do you know Kraljevic," and the statement that I recorded does represent that and the content of the exchange that we had on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any present and vivid recollection of any parts of the Kraljevic references?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Yes. While I was reading this statement that I took in February 1997, I recalled that at some point, he certainly said that Darko was not psychologically stable, and even the words that he used in Serbo-Croatian had some kind of a phonetic similarity with the words in the English language, and whatever he said was faithfully recorded in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked various questions about practice, and you referred to protocols that require the identification of what, in some jurisdictions, is called hearsay. Just this: When were those protocols introduced formally?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You've been asked by a question that used the word "selective" about what you put into these statements. If, in the course of answers given by the witness, material that is or might be exculpatory is mentioned, what's the practice in relation to such material?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: After a thorough discussion of the matter, it's absolutely going to be recorded as it is, without any addition or subtraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any question of being selective in the material that you put in these statements?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: Apart from one's basic sense of what's relevant and what's not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mujezinovic, in this statement, had it been read back to him?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: It was, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he then sign it?

utterances.speaker: EHSAN BAJWA
utterances.text: He did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask at the moment and probably all I'm going to ask. On the basis that the witness, subject to any questions of the Chamber, will be released, would the Chamber give him the warning about any other witnesses who may come here after? The witness Kehoe, if he's now required, is presently engaged in the last stages of another case, but he is, of course, in the same building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bajwa, thank you for coming to give evidence. You are released. The point that counsel was making was to tell you not to talk to any other prospective witnesses about your evidence, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will bear that in mind, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May he remain outside just for a minute to be technically released by one of my staff when I've raised one matter with the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm concerned to note that Mr. Sayers, who was here yesterday and who conducted the cross-examination of Mr. Mujezinovic but who isn't here today, has, in correspondence which is then reflected in argument to you, characterised witness statements built on Mujezinovic's evidence as "ad hoc compilations of what witnesses supposedly discussed with investigators, slanted in a manner to effect the accused's interests adversely." He went on to say: "They are the investigator's statements, rather than those of the witness, strictly speaking." Mr. Stein, in a letter of the 21st of May, again built on the Mujezinovic experience, categorised these statements as "unreliable and artificially engineered documents, for all the reasons highlighted in Dr. Mujezinovic's testimony." I have taken the view throughout that the absurd hyperbole by the Defence is unhelpful to this litigation, but I certainly take the view that if they wish to advance that sort of proposition, they should put it to this witness. I note they have got no where near that, and I will proceed from now on on the basis that those allegations are withdrawn unconditionally, and if they are not to be withdrawn, I would respectfully invite the Chamber to decide whether these are matters that ought to be put, for we really cannot proceed on matters of this importance with this sort of language when it's not backed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I, myself, regarded those sort of comments as forensic hyperbole, and unless I had seen something to demonstrate their truth, I would have disregarded them. I speak for myself, of course, entirely. I don't propose, unless anybody else wants me to, to have the witness back for those matters to be put. He's given his evidence quite clearly about what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you, Mr. Stein, want to have the witness back to put those sort of things to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, sir. His testimony is quite clear. Your Honours are left with a choice. You can believe Dr. Mujezinovic or you can believe the witness. There are certainly inconsistencies between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As you rightly say, those are entirely matters for the Trial Chamber to consider in due course. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'll ask for him to be further released from outside the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We are now going on to the argument, Mr. Smith, but before we do, there's one matter which I have in mind which I want to raise briefly. Mr. Nice, in your absence, a witness was called, and I made some comments to Mr. Scott which, no doubt, have been relayed to you, but I would wish them to be made again so that you could hear. Looking overall at the trial so far, we've had some 20 witnesses, five of them have dealt with events at Kaonik, and relying on the Rule 73 bis D, I think that there can be a reduction in evidence in relation thereto. Perhaps you could bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And no more at least, I hope, before the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will deal with that, and, indeed, Kaonik has yet to be discussed by us, save that I think I'm aware that we have to give some consideration to the places from which people were taken to Kaonik and dates, but that apart, there will be no resistance to Your Honour's observations, and thank you for making them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will give a brief introduction and deal with issues involving the law. My colleague, Mr. Stein, will deal with some of the practical issues raised by the Prosecutor's proposal and the specifics that you mentioned yesterday about fairness and this particular dossier. I think it is important at the outset to be clear about the issue before the Trial Chamber, and I believe my learned colleague has done that. The question is can major elements of a case before the ICTY, and these village attacks are major elements as I discussed yesterday, be tried on paper with unsworn witness statements and investigators' summaries, or, alternatively, will testimonial evidence be tested by questioning by the Defence an evaluation by the Trial Chamber of live, oral testimony by percipient witnesses? It is a matter, as I indicated yesterday, of very great significance to the Defence. Indeed, as I said at an earlier session, should such witness statements or reports by investigators be placed in evidence without the opportunity for cross-examination by the Defence, we would, with all respect, be obligated, I think, professionally obligated to appeal the matter immediately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, that is not a point to make before a Trial Chamber, a trial of first instance. Whether you appeal or not is of no relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will pass on. Let me turn to the argument in chief on the law, and I will deal firstly with the question of the problem facing the Trial Chamber. The problem is, one, the length of the trial and the scope of the material required by the indictment pled by the Prosecution. I suggest, as I did yesterday, that as this trial has gone on, there have been techniques developed and practices honed, and the Trial Chamber has exercised its own authority so that if the problem is not completely solved, it's largely solved, that is to say, the Trial Chamber, in our judgement, has the power and the ability to scope the trial as it needs to be done. I suggest that a major shift in procedures at this time would constitute changing horses in midstream. It would require a change, in our judgement, to both the Statute and the Rules and could not be done by the Trial Chamber alone. It would be disruptive. It would, in our judgement, not shorten the trial, and Mr. Stein will speak to this. It's risky. It shifts the Prosecutor's burden to the Defence. It is not the procedures that our client understood would be applied to him when he surrendered, when he chose counsel, and that is the reason that Rule 6(C) alone would prohibit application in this trial, even if the Statute or the Rules were changed to allow it. Dossiers, in our judgement, can be useful collations of evidence about a particular set of events, but the admission of witness statements or investigators' reports do not, in our judgement, further the search for truth, and this is true because the Judges themselves are prevented from probing, considering, and determining witness demeanour, witness credibility, witness background and potential bias, the nature and extent of witness observations, particularly the opportunity to observe percipient events, an event on a percipient basis, and this is particularly true where, I believe it has been demonstrated and Mr. Stein will discuss this, these witness statements are, I think, undeniably in some circumstances unreliable, and the investigator's report, as we have set out in our pleading on the Tulica dossier, is, in some regards, unreliable, and in any case, the witness statements proposed to be used by the Prosecutor are selective. She has selected one when there are many that she has omitted to use. As a result, it is our view that neither untested, unsworn witness statements, nor investigators' summaries are an acceptable substitute for testimonial evidence by a percipient witness. An admission of either would be a serious error. I turn first to the Statute and the Rules of the Tribunal. The Statute, fixed by the Security Council, Article 21(4)(e), the opportunity "to examine or have examined witnesses against him." I mentioned Rule 90(A) requiring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Rule --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Rule 21(4)(e), Your Honour, "Rights of the Accused." It is that language, that exact language, "to examine or have examined the witnesses against him," that is used in the International Covenant and the European Convention, and that is the subject of the case law that I will discuss before the European Court of Human Rights. Rule 90(A) of the Tribunal's Rules deals with and requires direct oral presentation of testimony as the normal way of doing business. Rule 90(B) requires that testimony be sworn and thus subject to perjury provisions of the Tribunal's Rules. I don't propose to go on with all of the various sections of the Rules that bear on this question, Your Honour, on the grounds that, number one, many of them have been discussed before in the context of the Aleksovski case and its ruling, and also they are in our materials, and in the interests of time, unless Your Honours have specific questions, I will turn to the question of the inconsistency of what the Prosecutor proposes with the normal civil law procedures. The key point with the civil law procedures, which the Prosecutor's proposal is designed to mimic and to adapt for purposes here, is one that I think we have pointed out, that is, testimony before an investigating judge at an early stage in a proceeding, while it can sometimes be used in a later trial before the judge of first instance, is normally sworn testimony taken by a judicial officer whose duty it is to be neutral, as opposed to unsworn testimony, not subject to the rules of perjury, but taken by a person whose duty it is to -- as the manual that we have cited in our brief clearly states, whose duty it is to prepare cases for the prosecuting attorney because they work for the prosecuting attorney. This is a very important set of distinctions, and it cannot be cured -- the difficulty, the issue cannot be cured by simply saying that this Court can sit as an investigating judge. First of all, the way that the civil law system would work, there would then be some other court of first instance in which the trial would take place, but this is the court in which the trial takes place. Secondly, the investigating judge himself listens to the oral testimony. The person that receives the statement without the oral testimony is the subsequent judge at the proceeding, and there the reliance is on the fact that at some stage in the proceeding, that is to say, in the early stage before the investigating judge, the Defence has had the opportunity to test and challenge the testimonial evidence by questioning a live witness, or at least by having the statement taken, sworn under the rules of perjury, and before a judicial officer. That is simply not the situation the Trial Chamber faces. It could have been, it could have been if the Tribunal had started out at the outset and deputised, in effect, investigating judges who were not part of the Prosecutorial force, who took statements in locations in Bosnia or in Kosovo. That is simply not the way the Tribunal is organised at this point. Let me turn then to why it is that the Prosecutor's proposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I understand that. You're saying that in the civil-law system, evidence is taken before an investigating judge. That evidence is normally sworn evidence and there is opportunity for cross-examination. That testimony is used later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is sworn testimony. It is subject, as I understand it, to the rules of perjury. I think it does sometimes involve

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: not. My colleague, Mr. Naumovski, and these other gentlemen are far greater experts. I'm not an expert indeed in the civil law. They know a great deal more about it. It may be used later before the trial judge, or it can be, in proper circumstances, generally extraordinary circumstances. The basic requirement and normal rule is the appearance of the witness, and these gentlemen can comment on that in more detail. The Prosecutor's proposal is also inconsistent, in our judgement, with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights that I've referred to and the European Convention on Human Rights, both of which use exactly or essentially the same language, "Examine or have examined witnesses against him." Let's turn to the case law involving the European Convention before the European Court of Human Rights, because it is the only case law at the international level which has construed these phrases. When you look at the case law, what you find is, and this is set out in our skeleton argument and in the attachment to the Prosecutor's response to Judge Robinson's concern about these cases, filed on June 17th, written by Mr. Stavros. There must be a witness to confront and question at some stage for a statement, written statement, of a witness not present at the trial itself to be taken into evidence, considered, and mainly, decisively, primarily, depends on the court, relied upon in making the judgement. Three cases were cited by the Prosecutor in its June 17th submission and response to Judge Robinson for the proposition that what they propose is permissible. All three cases were reversed for failure to have a witness attend the trial. The Barbera case, the Unterpertinger case, and the Bricmont case. Indeed most of the ECHR cases reverse for failure to have a life witness. Some of those do that even when there were questions asked by an investigating judge of a witness who later fails to show at trial. The Barbera case and the Kostovski case are examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't remember the facts of those cases, but certainly in some of the European cases the witness were absolutely crucial witnesses, witnesses who identified the accused and that sort of thing. There is a distinction, isn't there, between a witness on such a central issue and a witness who may deal with more peripheral matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would articulate it this way, Your Honour: I think it goes to the issue of mainly, decisively, or primarily relying but in a complex case with many of the elements of the offence. I would argue that any witness -- that the witness is -- the importance of the witness must be determined as to each element of the offence. If there's a necessary link and a witness testifying to it, whose testimony is crucial to that necessary element, such as an attack on a village, that is not a peripheral witness. It is the witness crucial to a crucial link. If there was a witness that was completely peripheral to an necessary element, that would be a different question but that's not what we're dealing with in these cases. We are dealing with witnesses who are usually to a necessary element. That's the point that I made yesterday, that each one of these village attacks is a necessary element in the Prosecutor's case. She need not have chosen to try to prove her case in 15 villages, but she has done so and we are obligated to defend in those 15 cases. The cases reverse even where there were investigators who took the statements available for cross-examination, and I cite the Delta case and the Kostovski case. One case made a particular point of saying unsworn testimony, unsworn statements are not appropriate. The cases reverse even when there is substantial corroborative evidence on occasion, such as the Unterpertinger case and Bricmont. Finally, the cases reverse even where there are countervailing, strong countervailing social policy considerations, such as, for example, the fight against organised crime and drugs, and I cite the Kostovski case and the Saidi case, or where terrorist activity is involved, and that's the Barbera case cited by the Prosecutors themselves. The few cases that do affirm have crucial facts that are not present here. So, for example, in the Isgro case and the Doorson case, adequate forms of confrontation at some stage, for example, an investigating judge with counsel present, with questions asked, some form critical of questions being asked, those facts are present. They have affirmed when there is a waiver by the defendant. The defendant simply doesn't raise the issue below. They have affirmed in some case where there is very significant other corroborative evidence that is probably before the Tribunal, but not in a case, obviously, where all of the witnesses on a critical link, like an attack on a particular village, are done on paper. Here we are dealing with, as I indicated before, written witness statements of questionable reliability, unsworn, no perjury penalty, untested by questioning by the Defence of indeed an equal arms issue in and of itself, and selectively included. We're dealing with summaries of witness statements by non-recipient investigators, in this case one who did not even speak to most of the witnesses. Let me turn briefly to the British law because Your Honours have raised that subject. This is obviously not matter on which I am an expert. Indeed, the first question is the Criminal Justice Act of 1988 that I think Judge Robinson may have referred to yesterday, and one provision of which, I believe, is involved in the case which the Judge was concerned about and was handed out this morning, before we began, by the Prosecutor. That act has two sections dealing with documentary evidence. One is section 23, dealing with first-hand hearsay in documents and, secondly, a section 26, much more relevant, dealing with statements prepared for criminal proceedings and involving, in the latter case, a presumption against admissibility, and investigators' reports that have statements by witnesses are clearly prepared in contemplation of criminal proceedings and maybe analogous to that provision where there is a presumption against their admission. There's another section that Your Honours, at least one of Your Honours will know far better than I as to its applicability, and that's the Criminal Justice Act 1967, section 9, which provides that a written statement by any person can be evidence but only if none of the parties objects within seven days of being served a copy. The case that Your Honour referred to yesterday, Judge Robinson, I've looked at. It seems to me that that case is helpful. It says that the Prosecutor, under English law, should have obtained a statement by the witness not present at the trial, "on commission," which I take is an English statement for letters rogatory or something of that sort, under section 3 of the 1980, I think, or '90 act, which would have allowed the Defence a right of cross-examination at the location, a foreign location, where that statement was to be taken. As a result, there was no, I think it's dicta, but there was no violation of the European Convention on Human Rights and the opportunity to cross-examine. As it turns out, the Prosecutor was not diligent in that case, and under British law the statement couldn't be used because he had not been, but I think it underlines the fact that to be consistent with the European Convention, there has to be an opportunity to challenge at some stage, as I indicated earlier. I might add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, Mr. Smith. I apologise for interrupting you but perhaps we can speed things up a little bit. If I understand you well, you would accept, according to this English jurisprudence, that the Prosecutor submits these statements on condition that you can call the witness to cross-examine him. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm afraid that that was not what I was saying, and I'm afraid that I would not be prepared to concur in that procedure. That has the effect of shifting the burden of going forward, and arguably the burden of proof, to the defendant, because the defendant must then call the witness. This is the Prosecutor's case. Our case will come later after the Prosecutor has rested, but we ought not have to bear burdens of putting the case on. That is the job of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) But what would be your conclusion from the English jurisprudence that you have quoted from? You are telling us that according to the Tribunal, the statements would be accepted on condition that the witnesses could be called, that is, the person who has made the statement would be called to cross-examine. Is that your conclusion or are you quoting that simply as a theoretical premise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have not made myself clear about the procedure that, as I understand it, was used in that case. There was a crime in the UK against a gentleman who resided in the United States, and that gentleman chose not to appear in the proceeding in the UK. The Prosecution could have used the conventions in English law, based on conventions, for going to the United States and obtaining a statement by that victim -- by this potential witness. If they had done that, the defence would have been entitled to go along and, under America law and law in many countries, would have been entitled to be present when the Prosecutor put the questions and to cross-examine the witness, just as he would have done if the witness would have appeared to trial. That was found to satisfy the obligation under the European Convention. What happened instead was that the Prosecution let that opportunity slip pass them and attempted to use at trial a written statement that they had obtained that had not gone through that procedure and to which the Defence had no opportunity to cross-examine, and that attempt, because they were negligent, was found, under English law alone, to be inapplicable, and that's why I said that the whole thing is simply dicta when it comes to the question of compliance with the European Convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will add, Judge Bennouna of course speaks for himself, but I thought he was asking you where would be the unfairness if the written statements were admitted subject to a right of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I attempted to answer it and I've obviously not succeeded, but I attempted to answer it by saying that that has the effect of shifting into the defendant's case, with the burden on the defendant, of calling witnesses, perhaps having to take them on direct-examination when they are likely to be adverse, since they are Prosecution witnesses, and for any number of reasons, and my colleague Mr. Stein will deal with this at length -- I'm almost finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand how that will result in a shifting of the burden, because it would be rather like, as far as I see it, the procedure set out in the Rules for expert statements or depositions. Statements can be admitted, but if you want to cross-examine, then you have the right to cross-examine. I don't understand how that results until an unfairness or shifts the burden.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't understand Your Honour's question. If what you're saying is that -- you're saying that the statement would be admitted as an expert report would be proffered for admission. The Defence would then say whether it chose to cross-examine, and if it chose to cross-examine, the Prosecutor would have to produce the witness in his case. That the hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I guess -- I think that works. That's essentially the way you treat an expert report and the introduction of an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go one stage further. Suppose we, although, were added this condition: The statement is admitted or the transcript is admitted subject to cross-examination by the Defence but there is added, on leave being given by the Court on the Defence showing cause, I think you would say, as to the reason why the witness has to be cross-examined. You will no doubt say that that is shifting a burden. It's no burden of proof, of course, all it is is an indication as to what the issues you want to raise with the witness are. So the question really is is there something on which we want to cross-examine? Apart from enunciating some general principle, we should be able to cross-examine who we want when there is nothing to be cross-examined to. Of course, that applies particularly in the case of transcripts, where in a similar case to this, witnesses have given evidence and been cross-examined, as happened in Aleksovski. Perhaps you'd like to think about that. It's about time we had a break anyway. Quarter after hour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to finish this afternoon at twenty-five past five. It would be helpful if we could finish this argument today, including Mr. Kovacic, if we can. I understand there is a matter you want to raise, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are a few administrative matters, one or two of which I have to deal with today, and they won't, I think, take just five minutes. I think, in reality, they are likely to take ten or fifteen minutes. I've also got already a number of things I would want to be able to just mention in reply to what Mr. Smith has already said. As to the administrative matters, I really can't put them off because they are timetable matters, and they have to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So they should be dealt with at ten past five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
