utterances.text: I would have thought that would be safer, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me go back for a moment to the question that Judge Robinson raised, because I want to be certain that there isn't a misunderstanding. I assumed that what the Judge was saying was that there would be a procedure in which a witness would come, give his direct testimony, but a witness statement could be introduced as an exhibit, in effect, and I think my counsel tell me -- co-counsel tell me think that that is not what Judge Robinson had in mind, and I see him shaking his head. Let me do the following then, if I may: Make two -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The procedure that I had in mind is modelled on the procedure for depositions and expert testimony. The witness statements would be admitted, subject to a right of cross-examination, but that latter part may be tailored, but that's my understanding of it, what I have in mind, that there would be a right of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Let me then amend my answer and say that we do believe that would present difficulties. Let me make two very quick points to finish up the discussion of the law, and we are now very much into practical matters, and I will turn over to my co-counsel, Mr. Stein, who will deal directly with your question and yours, Your Honour. Two quick points: On Yugoslav law, civil law jurisdiction, unsworn statements simply cannot be used in criminal proceedings. Even sworn statements taken before an investigative judge can only be used in exceptional circumstances and with the consent of both parties. Second point: The Kostovski case, and I would close on the law simply by quoting the judges of the European Court of Human Rights. This was a case involving organised crime, a case in which the witness did not appear and a witness statement was used, and it was reversed, even where the investigators were available to be cross-examined. The defendant had that opportunity, and I might read the language, Your Honours: "It is true that the Defence was able, both before the Utrecht District Court and the Amsterdam Court of Appeal, to question one of the police officers and both of the examining magistrates who had taken the declarations," and the language that I would like to leave you with on the law is where the judges of that European Court of Human Rights say: "The court does not underestimate the importance of the struggle against organised crime ... Although the growth in organised crime doubtless demands the introduction of appropriate measures, the government's submissions appear to the court to lay insufficient weight on what the applicant counsel described as 'the interest of everybody in a civilised society, in a controllable and fair judicial procedure'. The right to a fair administration of justice holds so prominent a place in a democratic society that it cannot be sacrificed to expediency." I will turn now to my co-counsel to deal with these more practical questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. I've thought long and hard about this issue. I've thought about it from our American experience, from what I have heard is the British experience, and just the reality, however, of the common experience. Of course, we can't just graft a system from common experience because there are rules to guide us, but in this very courthouse, in this very courtroom, we have some guidance. We have witnesses whose statements have been given to us, whose summaries have been given to us by the Prosecution, and in half a dozen instances, their testimonies, in a leading fashion, have deviated substantially from not just their pre-trial statements but from also their summaries. The two best experts on the subject have found -- or the three best experts, Mr. Lopez-Terres and Mr. Scott, when their witnesses either collapsed or just did not say what they were supposed to say, Witness H, Dr. Mujezinovic, departed radically from what was in their summary which, of course, was based on their statement and which was based on their proofing. When they departed radically from that, we made large argument about it, and that goes ultimately to the question you're asking. Also in this courtroom, we've had a witness who's denied he made a statement whatsoever, Mr. Surkovic. When I cross-examined him relative to Zenica and his appearance there based on the late delivery of that appearance, he said, "I wasn't even there. I don't remember anything about it." It could have been a pure failure of memory, as Judge Bennouna queried him, or alternatively, it could be something very different, I don't know the answer to that, but he didn't remember that 1994 court appearance before his friend who he said he has coffee with. That raises some suspicions. We've had in this very courtroom witnesses who, in their statements, say that Mr. Kordic is king, he is God in Busovaca, he did all manner of things, who, on inspection, on cross-examination, of course, say they have no basis for that. The essence of what I'm saying are the three Cs: Confrontation, cross-examination, and credibility. We also have had witnesses in this courtroom who have testified maybe perfectly consistently with their pre-trial statements, consistent with what the Prosecution expects but who you don't have to believe, for whatever the reason, pure credibility. Three examples I can think of: Mr. Cicak, as he sat here with his demeanour and the way in which he wanted to run the courtroom, Mr. Zlotrg, who because of all the issues in his own personal life feels there's a major conspiracy between men, women, and children of the Croat nationality. You don't have to believe all or part of what they say. Pure credibility issues. A witness, I don't know his designation, I can't remember, whose witness statement was replete with the word "Ustasha." That raises an issue of his credibility as well. So if we keep the three Cs with us at all times, and you know that those three Cs came to us historically, then I think what I'm about to say hopefully will make sense. Let me answer directly why just putting the witness on the stand, having the witness statement, and then cross-examining would not be fair. It wouldn't be fair for the defendant, Defence counsel, or the Court, and it would not be fair because the Court would be deprived of the witness's direct testimony as he gives it. You would not be able to hear and make a determination, as the Prosecution presents it, how the witness's demeanour and credibility is, whether or not he appears, as he is giving his narrative, to be credible to you. Moreover, the accused and Defence counsel would not have the then present ability to hear the accusation against the accused in a language the accused and Defence counsel can understand, to have the confrontation of the witness. Instead, we would be left, even if the Prosecution produced the witness, thereby not having the burden of a production problem, even if the Prosecution produced the witness, we would have to presume either that he has testified consistently with his witness statements and then examine, or alternatively, ask him, irrespective of the witness statements, what his version of the facts are. I don't think that's going to be faster, and we will have, therefore, the situation confounding us of we have to do the direct examination. We will pretend that that paper doesn't exist called the witness statement and say, "What did you see?" So I think I've answered your question directly, Judge Robinson. I'm trying to. If we always focus on those three things, then it's apparent. Now, again, I've struggled with this because I'm saying who has a monopoly on truth? I do agree with Mr. Nice. Our system doesn't, nor does he. Frankly, if the process that Mr. Nice talked about yesterday, that is, engrafted into the English system, were grafted into our system, the Defence lawyer would be guilty not only of malpractice, he might be disbarred, but we don't have to win. We don't have to win the debate of which system is better or worse. The common experience of these statements is what's important. As they're generated, there are 150 or 200 folks from the Prosecutor's office who take statements. That's part of the issue. They do the best they can. As two human beings in different languages sit there and try to communicate, the process of communication is different. There's a second statement, sometimes a third. There are also statements from Zenica. There are a compilation of statements, and each of the folks tries to get it right, but all of that out-of-court work, of course, is never presented to Your Honours. There is no videotape going. There is no audiotape going. It can't be. It is a summation as best as Mr. Bajwa and anyone else can do it, but nonetheless within the limits of time, within the limits of the collective knowledge of the individuals who are taking the statement, within the limits of the circumstances. Sometimes that creates closer to the versions, sometimes not. We know in this very courtroom, based on two expert opinions, one being Mr. Scott and one being Mr. Nice, that that process has flaws. For instance, Mr. Scott the other day, in discussing the issue of a witness statement, a witness summary which had many new additions to it, raised the dilemma before Your Honour that every witness who is proofed, formed, interviewed pre-trial adds more. I don't doubt that for a minute. I jumped up and agreed with that. Every witness who I have prepared for trial adds more or deletes or clarifies or is inconsistent to whatever the party is, be it exculpatory or inculpatory. That's the real experience, the trial experience. Consequently, the Prosecution, and the reference to this is in day 39, July 8, pages 4482 to about 4484, I won't read them, the Prosecution was quite clear that it was in a dilemma as to how to proceed. Anyone who is put on as a witness is in that same dilemma. So if we just limit ourselves to witness statements, the Court will be deprived of truth. The Court will be deprived of the additional evidence that the witness has to give or the witness's recantation of evidence he's already given by way of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You would be able to extract that in cross-examination. You would still be able to cross-examine the witness as to previous statements and inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The process you describe would still allow us to look at inconsistencies, but in the real terms and the real world, the witness takes the stand and either, A, testifies completely consistent with his out-of-court declarations, in which case there is no inconsistency, B, testifies inconsistently helpful to the accused, in which case there's no cross-examination. There were instances in this very trial where the witness departed from his statement or recanted it in the direct, and so there was no need to cross. If I may go back to my point, and that is we know the witnesses here are very different than no matter how well they are proofed or formed, and I might say, in the civil system, as opposed to the criminal system, even where we take depositions, extensive pre-trial procedures, this happens. Surprise happens all the time in courtrooms, but in a criminal case, the surprise is more important. So it always has to go both ways. The second expert, frankly, is Mr. Nice. Since he quotes from me, I'd like to quote from him. In a letter between us dated 24 June: "There may always be amplifications and some corrections, but the plain fact is that these statements were made at a time when memories were fresher than they now are and when the witness did not have the pressure of facing lawyers and defendants by whom they are sometimes affected in various ways." I agree with that. That's called a right to confront. You just can't say in civilised society, "You did this" and walk away. You have to come in here and look at the man you are potentially sending to gaol, on your evidence, for life and let him hear you say it, and when that confrontation exists, according to my expert, Mr. Nice, there are differences. The witnesses do break down. In the direct examination, the process of a witness statement just being introduced would eliminate that altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you, at some stage, address these two points, Mr. Stein? 1) The examples you've given relate maybe to crucial witnesses who have given evidence about the direct involvement with your client. The other point I would wish you to address is this, that there is a distinction between the written statement and a transcript of evidence which has been subject to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witnesses whose statements, it's being suggested, should be introduced or whose transcript should be introduced are not those who deal directly with your client, and part of the process, I don't know whether you've directed your mind to this or not, part of the process is to try and see what is in issue and what isn't. But if at the end of the case we find that we've spent many weeks listening to evidence which wasn't in issue, it will be a considerable waste of public time and money, so the earlier we can clarify the issues, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's actually three, and let me address them in reverse because my mind will work that way. There's no question that the current process, and this is my humble opinion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By the way, I've got a fourth: It says, "Kindly slow down for the record."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: A dilemma, but be done by ten after five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you can't finish by then, we will simply have to adjourn the matter. It would be useful if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I will do my best, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, if may I assist? Could we focus, in reality, on what affects us? Because we aren't about to deal with general problems, and I wish to assure Mr. Smith that we are working within the framework of the established rules. We're in the process of seeing, together with you and with your agreement, to what extent for questions that do not directly affect the accused, questions regarding the surroundings and regarding facts that occurred here and there and which normally are noted and fit within the regular system in the country, could we use the procedure in accordance with 94 bis, referring to expert witnesses, or 93 ter because 93 ter has to do with depositions under oath. Perhaps we could ask for an oath to be taken for this or that statement. This is a statement that would corroborate testimony on this or that fact under the reservation that there is cross-examination. When we mentioned the example of an expert witness, Mr. Smith said, "Yes," but after the break, he retraced his position. So let us concentrate on this. When we are dealing with repetitive matters, for instance, for Kaonik, we have already had five, and also for other villages, there have been several, you yourself have proposed that two witnesses per village would be sufficient. We could also have such a procedure with two witnesses if other witnesses corroborate what has been said by the first. Then we could provide these statements in a similar way as expert statements, which would corroborate what has already been said. If you have any trouble over those subsequent statements, you would inform the Chamber of this. If the Chamber is convinced of the fact that you are right about it, then we can look at it. This only applies to 12, 13, 14 villages. Let us concentrate ourselves by trying to limit the number of witnesses per village. That is where we stand, and I think questions, theoretical questions regarding the civil law, the common law, nobody believes in this contradiction anyway, but we are an International Tribunal without a state behind us, as you know well. So that is where we stand. Let us try and focus on practical issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I'll try. Consistent with the Rules, Your Honours, of course, can limit the Prosecution or the Defence to the number of witnesses. You can limit the length of the examination. Now, that raises the issue, quite candidly, of jurisprudence that we don't need to address of how much involved the Tribunal wants to get in the presentation of evidence. Under the current rules, the Judges tremendously involved. Tremendously involved. So that's a given and it's within your right. The short answer to your question, of course, is that you can exercise your control that way, consistent with the Rules, without anyone being allowed to complain. In this particular case, sure, if you want to put on a witness familiar with the terrain, the population, these are percipient witnesses, he's been there, but when he incorporates by whole cloth the witness statement that's a different departure. Let me point out, while I'm standing and before I forget, this dossier, and I'd like to have the usher pass this out, contains half a dozen or so -- seven witnesses who have given a variety of statements. Those statements -- what we're handing up now is self-created by us. It's what the OTP has not included in the dossier. It's the other dates of the witness statements, the other statements given to various investigators and Tribunals. Those statements, when put together, look like this, about three-quarters of an inch of material. As you can see, some are much closer in time to the events. So I just wanted to, before I forgot and got off track again, that the dossier, as presently constituted, is incomplete, and the point Mr. Smith made but what I wanted to graphically show you. Judge, with regard to important versus non-important witnesses, to be sure that distinction can be made, at first blush it seems very real, and as I was thinking about that yesterday, my response has to be twofold. The Prosecution's case of conspiracy, criminal association, aiding and abetting is so broad that it literally encompasses all of the actors in the drama that we've been talking about. You've heard that, that Mr. Scott wanted to bring in great evidence about Mr. Sliskovic and other individuals because it is their contention that they were under Mr. Kordic's control. So what appears at first blush sometimes to be a non-important issue on a non-important fact with a non-important player may, in the grand scheme of things, become important. I must say that as we unfold this case, that which appeared unimportant to me and to us at the beginning becomes more important as we go on and vice verse, as the evidence unfolds. A lot of what I'm saying in response to your question may well be resolved with a rule change relative to discovery, and large amounts of discovery pre-trial and well in advance of trial. I can think of all kinds of systems in which discovery is brought in the criminal context, with the goal to shorten trials, but those aren't the rules that we have now. There are jurisdictions where you can take depositions in criminal cases, and that than might be a way. That might lead to some of the shortening issues that we are here talking about, but under the rules as constituted now, that doesn't happen. Your Honour also -- well, I think that was two of the three. I think I missed one. Yes, transcripts. Transcripts, of course, are a much closer case, because -- and pre-Aleksovski, I would have acknowledged they were a closer case as long as the issues are relatively close, and the same under Aleksoviski were left with that holding which I know Your Honour is familiar with. So that's the rule relative to transcripts. In this dossier, the transcripts aren't necessary because they're cumulative. We've already heard one of the witnesses, the other is unavailable, and then you get into the unavailability issue, which brings me to another point. I make all these nice notes, I have an order to these things, but they never come out that way. We reject out of hand any implication by the Prosecution that when a witness is unavailable it's of because anything the accused did. Witnesses are unavailable for a host of reasons. Their stated desire not to come being not necessarily any fault of the accused, being instead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That allegation has not been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, it hasn't been made directly, and if it's made inferentially I want to stop it now, but they don't come, and why, I don't know. It may well be that, on reflection, they don't want to confront the accused or they don't want to live up to the story that they told. The Prosecution would take advantage of that and use evidence that historically is less satisfactory and furthers the search for truth less. Let me make an argument that is a pure argument but I think it has some persuasive effect. You could theoretically construct -- I guess this goes to Judge Bennouna's question. You could construct a situation in which the complete trial is trial by dossier-type witnesses. You could construct it through villages. Theoretically you could just have the Prosecution stand up and give a summary of the case and we could cross-examine somehow that. Theoretically you could have a system where the indictment is proof that there's a crime and the burden shifts to the Defence. You could do all that. That would be, of course, violation of statutory rules in this Tribunal and fundamental rights under International Law, and it wouldn't be a better system. It may be more expeditious but it wouldn't be better, because you who have to make a decision about a man's future would not have the benefit of seeing the persons who are making the accusations. You would be getting the story twice, third time, fourth, fifth-hand removed. So we can craft all manner of things and do all things but it wouldn't make our system better. We are constrained by the rules as they exist and by the Statutes on human rights. Parenthetically -- I was thrown off track -- there are, in this very situation, instances in which the Defence and the Prosecution have indeed cooperated. I don't want to stand up here any more and hear that we haven't in some ways cooperated. We have, for instance gone over the core documents. There's an ongoing discussion about what will be admitted without any problem, and if we can resolve our issues relative to objections, we'll do so. We're going to be meeting with the Prosecution shortly to resolve issues of exhibits. It's in everyone's interests along those lines, but we are limited by what's fair, what's right, and what our client's expectation of our role is. We are here -- the Defence role is to scrutinise, and it may make it slower at times. Our Defence role is to view with a jaundiced eye, and that's my last point, view with a jaundiced eye what the witnesses say. When we read a witness statement, it's with the defence in the back of my mind and it's with where we want to go. With respect, when we read a witness statement, we read it differently than when the Court does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, I think the comment was unfortunate that you are limited by the expectations of your -- of your client's expectations of what your role should be. I don't think the Chamber is so limited. I think what your role is independent of your client's expectations. That's dictated by a professional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No question about it. There are limits to the client's expectation and there are realms in which we operate independently. I painted, as I am sometimes wont to do, with too broad a brush, but the client, to echo what Mr. Smith said, voluntarily surrendered himself to this Tribunal based on its rules and it's process. He could have very well chosen different lawyers more familiar with the continental system or a different set of rules. He chose not to. I again caution, and I want to say this in a non-controversial way, the Court from anything that you decide, involving in a way that appears, even though it isn't, to favour one side or the other. I know, without any doubt, that to a moral certainty the Court is going to be fair to all sides. I don't doubt that for a second. But the appearance, of course, of what you do is also important, and it might appear that in the rush to avoid a two and half year trial we're forgetting things. It might appear that preliminary judgements have been made for us or against us, for the Prosecution or against the Prosecution, and in the rush to move forward we are forgetting process. I, again, to a moral certainty, do not believe you have made your choices and made your decisions. You have not. But since Mr. Nice alluded to it, the rest of the world, of course, watches and is watching how we proceed here, and it is an honour to proceed with that. I was going to start with that but I always get thrown off by my own thoughts. It's an honour to proceed here. It's an honour to be among men and women who are struggling to create a system that is fair given the realities of the issues on the ground. It truly is. It's an honour even to do battle with Mr. Nice, even though he may not like some of my invective. But I suggest the last American homily which I hopefully think will help the Court, and that is that the grist of justice grinds slowly but exceedingly fine and sometimes the search for truth just takes time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we're looking at the clock. How long do you think you're going to be? I don't want to put you under pressure of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult to say because we did not, unfortunately, coordinate our efforts. However, we were thinking more or less on the same lines, and now I have to omit some parts because certainly I will not repeat what my distinguished colleague says. If I may suggest, perhaps I could be finished in say 10 minutes or something, I guess, and then if there is a lot which I was not able to tell, perhaps you will give me tomorrow another 10 minutes or 15 minutes. Not more than, that I'm sure. Or simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not here tomorrow. Mr. Nice, how long are you going want to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Reply will be at least 15 minutes but it will be more compact if I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. Ten to fifteen minutes. Fifteen minutes probably. It will be more compact if prepared, typed, and reduced to a skeleton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kovacic, we'll adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- until next week to give a chance to complete your argument. Mr. Nice, if you would put yours in a skeleton. We'll have to find suitable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The administrative matters that I'm sorry I have to trouble you with can start off with something that is very simple. Can we distribute the expert summaries? To assist the Chamber and my learned friends for the defendants, I have prepared succinct overviews for the two witnesses. They aren't summaries in the sense that they don't follow what have been described as proofing sessions, so they are without-prejudice overviews by us of the critical passages for the Prosecution of those two reports, and they are, as the Chamber will see, indeed succinct. I hope they will help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you going to apply to ask any questions in chief of these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With your leave and given the brevity with which I have presented their material in this synopsis, I will seek probably to ask them a few questions in chief but I wouldn't forecast being very long, particularly given the way I'm focusing their material through these documents. There may be some other points of focus that will occur between now and Monday, but given the focus that we've presented. I would hope that I may be allowed at least to touch on the points of particular concern with them if I seek to do so. Now, the next matter concerns witnesses for the following week. That witness is a witness who was subject to a ten-day disclosure order and, therefore, I must disclose such material as I have about that witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the week after next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. Now, that witness is subject to an order of protection, a particularly tight order of protection by the court, and it's the first time that this order of protection has come into play, because although it may have been an order expressed to be effective for other witnesses, in those earlier cases the material about the witnesses had been distributed already and, therefore, the particularly tight terms of the protective order could not apply. So point number one, and without naming the witnesses because we're still in open session -- there's perhaps no reason why we shouldn't go into private session. I think these all are matters that would be safer dealt with in private session because of the risk of naming people who should otherwise not be named. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
